source.title: Language Models Can Predict Their Own Behavior

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some figures and parts of appendix figures are garbled in the extracted text.
record.tranche_reason: The study probes input-token hidden states to predict later outputs and behaviors, but does not use the rhyme-planning intervention or directly test causal steering of intervening text.
record.gate_note: The paper reports future-output prediction through probes. It does not test rhyming verse, candidate rhyme representations, or interventions on such representations. CoT cost and accuracy results are included where they report performance from the probe’s prediction of the final class; broader format and safety behavior-prediction results are retained as related findings. Values used only to select a layer or other hyperparameter are not separately recorded.
record.test_reason: Linear probes on Llama3.1-8B's final input-token state predict the class the model outputs after a CoT explanation, many tokens later. This is a probing test of V2's future-output decodability. Two caveats: the target is the final answer class, not exact token identity at set offsets, and the class may be readable from input features (e.g. sentiment) rather than from a model-internal plan. The format, safety and confidence probes predict output properties, not future tokens, so they fit no version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that input-token hidden states contain information about behaviour over the whole eventual output, enabling conformal early-warning and early-exit probes (65% CoT cost reduction, 91% jailbreak reduction). They add that probes generalize OOD and improve with model scale. Limits they report: longer outputs are harder, tasks needing external knowledge (answer correctness) fail, and layer choice is task-specific.
record.recipe_differences: Uses linear probes and conformal prediction to estimate eventual output classes or behaviors from input-token states; it does not use future-token lens decoding or causal interventions on candidate future tokens.
record.method_sensitivity: Probe performance varies with input-token position, probing layer, model size, task, confidence threshold, and output length. The authors state that early input tokens perform near randomly, larger models perform consistently better, and no general mid-versus-late layer pattern holds.

fits_no_version.finding: Input-state probes predict format-following failure, abstention failure on unanswerable and jailbreak prompts, and the model's eventual confidence (perplexity or verbalized). They fail to predict whether an MCQ answer will be incorrect.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Input hidden states encode some global properties of the eventual output (format compliance, refusal, confidence), but not its correctness relative to external truth.

record.problems: The study does not causally intervene on the predicted future content, and its principal results concern classification or behavioral properties rather than exact future-token prediction. Several detailed values are presented in figures whose extracted text is garbled; safety experiments do not name the model in the relevant section/table. Prediction performance varies by task and input position, and is near random for some targets.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for every format-following or confidence-estimation dataset/metric because the text gives only aggregate descriptions or the corresponding figure values are not recoverable from the extracted text. Figure-only model-family robustness results in Appendix A are not separately rowed because the plots are garbled and the text gives no per-model numerical values.

untested.parts: Exact-token prediction at specified offsets; any distance sweep. Only the final answer class after CoT is predicted.
Not studied: no rhyming verse and no intervention.
Not studied: no test of whether features are computed for later use.
Not studied: no rhyme planning in open models.
Not studied: no causal look-ahead in reasoning, chess or Sokoban.
No test of whether the decodable answer is a plan that steers generation or an input-level heuristic.

missing.what: OOD OpenBookQA result: 68% inference-cost reduction with 0.4% accuracy loss, training only on other MCQA datasets
Minimum inference-cost reduction of 4.7% on some dataset, meaning the probe is confident on few instances there. This matters for how general the decodability is.
Layer ablation: early layers give poor consistency; whether mid or late layers are better depends on the task
Mistral-7B-Instruct and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B replications, which the text says hold robustly (figure-only; declared in rows_left_out but no qualitative row)

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. The V2 evidence concerns the final classification answer, many tokens ahead, not exact next-k tokens. The answer class may be largely determined by input semantics, so decodability here does not imply internal planning. The CSQA/CosmoQA discrepancy for Fig. 5 right should be checked. The safety rows (r12–r14) do not name the model.

versions.untested_parts: No rhyming-verse task, candidate-rhyme readout, or intervention changing a rhyme ending.
The study predicts final classes and other output properties from input states; it does not evaluate exact-token prediction at specified future offsets or provide a several-token distance sweep.
No test distinguishes features computed for later positions from features arising as a byproduct of next-token prediction.
No rhyme-planning test or open attribution-graph analysis.
CoT classification is evaluated, but no causal look-ahead planning is tested; chess, Sokoban, and other architectures are not studied.

The paper reports limits on prediction consistency and accessibility, but does not test whether future information is merely local next-token features or heuristics, or whether it causally steers generation.

rows.check: Measures the study's own early-exit method against vanilla CoT. Cost reduction mixes conformal coverage with probe agreement, so it is an indirect proxy for decodability. Keep it as the main V2 evidence, but read it as method performance.

relationships.condition: Llama3.1-8B, final input-token state at layer 18, CoT text classification across 27 datasets (IID and OOD); also Llama3 3B/8B/70B scale sweep
relationships.reason: Probes predict the eventual post-CoT answer well enough to exit early with ≤1.34% IID and 2.3% OOD accuracy loss (r1–r3). Consistency rises toward the final tokens (r5) and with model size (r7).
relationships.display_finding: Early exits based on predicted final answers lost at most 1.34% IID accuracy and 2.3% OOD accuracy; consistency increased toward final tokens and with model size.

relation.reason: The study tests whether input-token representations predict eventual output content and behavior, including the class emitted after a reasoning chain.

tranche.reason: Linear probing directly investigates information about eventual output in input-token states, using answer-class prediction rather than general future-token decoding.

source_check.notes: Evidence concerns later answer labels and behavior attributes, without causal evidence for planning. Appendix C.2 binarizes MCQ and sentiment tasks; the CSQA/CosmoQA discrepancy remains unresolved.

statements.correction: First-quarter question-token probes: near-random eventual-answer prediction. Later positions: increasing consistency, with a sharp rise near final tokens. Consistency versus output length correlation: −6.1%. Body dataset: CSQA; Figure 5 caption dataset: CosmoQA.
statements.problem: The study establishes position-dependent probe performance, not that future content exists only at later positions. Early question positions also lack the remaining question input.
